analysis.one_liner: Bans commercial logging on federal public lands and retrains timber workers who lose their jobs.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan group of 61 House members backed a bill to end taxpayer-funded commercial logging on federal lands, but it never got a committee vote and died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have ended commercial logging and timber sales on national forests, national parks, wildlife refuges, and Bureau of Land Management lands, with a two-year phase-out for existing contracts. The bill's findings, citing Forest Service and GAO reports, argue the federal logging program loses taxpayer money every year — logging on federal lands supplies under five percent of U.S. timber while, per a Forest Service study, recreation and tourism on the same lands generate more than thirty times the jobs and income. In its place, the bill would create restoration crews to repair logging damage, fund fire-prevention work near homes, retrain displaced timber workers, and make permanent federal payments to rural counties and schools.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who the bill's findings say absorb an annual net loss from a logging program that returns only a fraction of what it costs. Rural counties and school districts, whose federal payments under the Secure Rural Schools Act would become permanent. People who live near or use federal forests, who would get fire-protection funding focused on making homes near forests fire-resistant rather than logging far from them. Timber workers who lose jobs would get retraining grants, job-search and relocation allowances, and hiring preference in the new restoration corps.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers, forest users, and rural counties

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits new timber sales on all federal public lands and ends commercial logging after a two-year phase-out of existing contracts, with the government paying out terminated contracts [S2][S3].

Redirects federal logging spending — capped at two-thirds of what logging cost taxpayers in the prior five years — into a Natural Heritage Restoration Corps that would decommission roads, remove invasive species, and use prescribed fire to reduce severe wildfire risk [S3].

Provides worker retraining grants, needs-related payments, and job-search and relocation allowances for timber workers laid off because of the ban, funded up to $80 million in the first year and $120 million in the third [S3].
Amends the Secure Rural Schools and Community Self-Determination Act to make education and road payments to rural counties containing federal land permanent rather than expiring in 2006 [S2][S3].

Up to $15 million annually would help owners of homes near federal forests reduce the flammability of their structures, and up to $100 million would fund development of non-wood paper and construction alternatives [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Timber companies and mills that buy federal timber would lose that supply, and logging and mill workers would lose jobs tied to federal timber sales — though the bill funds retraining and hiring preferences to cushion the transition. Taxpayers would fund restoration and retraining, but at a capped, lower level than the current logging program. Consumers could see modest wood-price effects, though federal timber supplies under five percent of U.S. consumption.

drawbacks.text: Federal timber is a small share of U.S. supply, but for individual mills and logging towns in the Pacific Northwest and elsewhere, losing it can be an existential local shock; retraining money does not rebuild a town's economy [S2][S3].

The bill sharply restricts mechanical thinning — it bars removal of the forest canopy and bans road construction for any fire-prevention project — relying mainly on prescribed fire and manual work, which some fire scientists and land managers argue limits the tools available to reduce hazardous fuels in dense forests [S3].
Terminating existing timber contracts early would require payments to purchasers, an immediate taxpayer cost before the promised savings arrive [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: end a program the bill documents as a net drain on taxpayers and a source of ecological damage, and spend less money restoring the land and helping the workers displaced. The transition costs for timber towns are real and only partially addressed, and the tight limits on thinning could hamper fuel reduction in some forests. But the fiscal case — GAO reports cited in the bill show timber sale receipts returning only a small fraction of program costs — and the worker-retraining provisions make this a serious, if ambitious, attempt to both protect public lands and not abandon the people whose jobs depended on logging them.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees and then five subcommittees, none of which ever held a markup or vote, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced July 25, 2005 by Rep. James Leach, a Republican, with 60 cosponsors — 59 Democrats and one other Republican [S1][S4].
It was referred to the Resources, Agriculture, and Education and the Workforce committees on the day of introduction [S1][S5].

Between August and October 2005 it was referred to five subcommittees, including the Forestry subcommittee; no committee or subcommittee ever reported the bill, held a recorded vote, or brought it to the floor [S5].
The bill received no further action before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Timber companies kept their access to federally subsidized timber sales, and the taxpayer-funded logging program the bill targeted continued unchanged. Rural counties kept waiting for the permanent payments the bill would have secured.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Timber companies and the existing logging program

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — a Republican lead sponsor, 59 Democratic cosponsors, and one additional Republican [S4] — but no vote was ever taken, so the partisan shape of the opposition was never recorded.

industries.note: The bill ends their access to federal timber sales, which the bill's findings say cost taxpayers far more than they return, and requires buyout payments on terminated contracts. The industry's gain under the status quo runs against taxpayers and public-land users.

The bill's findings cite a Forest Service study finding recreation and tourism on national forests generate over 30 times the jobs and income of federal logging. Unlogged, restored forests support that economy.

industries.industry: Wood-substitute and nonwood paper and construction products
industries.note: The bill directs up to $100 million in EPA grants toward developing nonwood alternatives for paper and construction, creating a research and market foothold for these products.
